rows: Two colours (say red & violet) focus together

questions.question: Q1. Define a pure spectrum and how to obtain one.
questions.answer: A pure spectrum is one in which a single color (monochromatic) appears, without overlapping colors or white. Use a prism + a narrow slit to isolate one wavelength; otherwise a 'simple spectrum' has color mixtures.
questions.shortcut: Single-wavelength → pure spectrum; prism + slit isolates.
questions.example: A prism gives a simple (broad) spectrum; a slit gives pure.

questions.question: Q2. Define dispersive power and its significance.
questions.answer: Dispersive power ω = (δ_v − δ_r)/δ_m, the ratio of the difference in violet and red deviations to the mean deviation. It measures how effectively a prism/lens separates colors; flint glass has a larger ω.
questions.example: Flint glass disperses colors more than crown glass.

questions.question: Q3. Explain chromatic aberration and spherical aberration.
questions.answer: Chromatic aberration is due to the wavelength-dependence of refractive index; different colors focus at different points, causing colored fringes. Spherical aberration is due to the use of spherical surfaces: marginal and paraxial rays focus at different points, giving a blurred image.
questions.shortcut: Chromatic = color focus error; spherical = ray-angle focus error.
questions.example: A simple lens shows color fringes (chromatic) and blur (spherical).

questions.question: Q4. How are chromatic aberration and spherical aberration corrected? (mention two.)
questions.answer: Chromatic: combine two lenses of different materials (crown + flint) to make an achromatic doublet. Spherical: use aspherical (parabolic) mirrors/lenses or a stop to use only paraxial rays; or apodize with a small aperture.
questions.shortcut: Achromatic doublet for chromatic; aspheric/stop for spherical.
questions.example: A photographic lens is an achromatic doublet.

questions.question: Q5. Define angular and linear magnification and when each is useful.
questions.answer: Linear magnification m = h'/h = −v/u (ratio of image and object sizes); angular magnification M = angle image subtends / angle object subtends. Linear is for real-size images (e.g. telescope, camera); angular is for instruments where image sizes are not directly comparable (e.g. magnifying glass).
questions.example: A magnifying glass has high M and small m.

questions.question: Q6. A lens has P = +4 D and another has P = +2 D in contact. Find the combined power and focal length.
questions.answer: For thin lenses in contact, powers add: P_total = 4+2 = 6 D, f = 1/6 ≈ 0.167 m = 16.7 cm (converging). ▥ 18.1–18.2 Pure Spectrum & Aberrations  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Pure Spectrum vs Ordinary (White) Spectrum Chromatic vs Spherical Aberration ▣ 18.3 Achromatism & Applications

questions.question: Q7. State the condition for an achromatic doublet of two prisms/lenses.
questions.answer: For achromatism, the net deviation for two colors must be zero while the net dispersion is not: (n_F−1)A + (n_C−1)A' = 0, or (ωA+ω'A') = 0 (for two chosen colors). For two thin lenses: (f_F−f_C)+ (f'_F−f'_C) = 0; equivalently 1/f_achrom = ω(1/f + 1/f').
questions.example: A crown + flint pair is an achromat.

questions.question: Q8. Explain an achromatic lens and why it is used in cameras.
questions.answer: An achromatic lens is a combination of a converging crown-glass and a diverging flint-glass lens (or the reverse) chosen so that chromatic aberration for two colors is eliminated while preserving dispersion. This sharpens color detail, so it is used in cameras and microscopes.
questions.shortcut: Crown + flint cancels two-color chromatic error.
questions.example: Your phone camera lens uses an achromat.

questions.question: Q9. How does a prism spectroscope work?
questions.answer: White light through a slit enters a prism; dispersion separates wavelengths into a spectrum (minimum-deviation position), and a telescope with a scale at the eyepiece measures each line's minimum deviation to identify wavelengths (compare with known values).
questions.shortcut: Prism + slit + telescope + scale; measure δ_m per color.
questions.example: Each spectral line's δ_m identifies its wavelength.

questions.question: Q10. What is a Fraunhofer line? Give an example.
questions.answer: Fraunhofer lines are dark absorption lines in the solar spectrum caused by elements in the sun absorbing specific wavelengths. The D-line (yellow) is sodium (D₁, D₂ ≈ 589 nm), used in spectroscopy.
questions.shortcut: Spectral absorption lines; D-line = sodium yellow.
questions.example: The D line lets one identify sodium in stars.

questions.question: Q11. Why is a prism preferred to a diffraction grating for high-resolution work?
questions.answer: A diffraction grating gives more orders and higher angular dispersion per unit than a prism for high-resolution work; for short wavelengths (UV/X-ray) a grating works better, while a prism is simpler for the visible with a continuous, monotonic spectrum. ▥ 18.3 Achromatism & Applications  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Achromatism: Two-Lens Pair PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: Grating: higher dispersion, multi-order; prism: simple, continuous.
questions.example: A high-resolution spectrometer uses a grating.

theoryItems.question: [State] T1. State the conditions for an achromatic doublet.
theoryItems.answer: For two thin lenses (materials of different dispersion) to be achromatic for two colors (e.g. F and C), their combined power must be the same for both: (n_F−1)/f_1 + (n_C−1)/f_1 = (n_F−1)/f_2 + (n_C−1)/f_2, giving the achromatic condition (ω/ f_1 + ω′/ f_2) = 0 while the net power is nonzero.
theoryItems.example: Used in a crown + flint doublet.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T2. Compare a prism and a diffraction grating as spectrosopes.
theoryItems.answer: A prism gives a continuous, monotonic spectrum with good resolution in the visible but poor at short (UV/X-ray) wavelengths and a single order. A grating gives multiple orders, higher and linear dispersion, and works into UV/X-ray; the price is overlapping orders (need a filter).
theoryItems.shortcut: Grating: higher dispersion, multi-order; prism: simple, monotonic.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T3. Explain chromatic aberration and how it is corrected.
theoryItems.answer: Because refractive index depends on wavelength, a simple lens forms different-colored images at different foci (violet closer, red farther), causing colored fringes. Correction uses an achromatic doublet: a converging crown lens plus a diverging flint lens chosen so two colors focus together, greatly reducing the fringing.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T4. Explain spherical aberration and how it is reduced.
theoryItems.answer: Marginal rays (far from the axis) of a spherical surface focus at a different point than paraxial rays, blurring the image. It is reduced by using aspherical (parabolic) surfaces, by a smaller aperture (stop) using only paraxial rays, or by combining surfaces of different shapes.
theoryItems.example: A small aperture sharpens a lens (higher f-number).

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain a pure spectrum and how a prism gives a 'simple' vs 'pure' spectrum.
theoryItems.answer: A pure spectrum shows one wavelength at a time (no overlap). A prism gives a 'simple' spectrum that is not pure, because different colors have different angular spreads; to obtain a pure (monochromatic) spectrum a narrow slit plus a second prism (or a lens) is used to isolate a single line.
theoryItems.shortcut: Prism alone → simple (mixed) spectrum; + slit/lens → pure.
theoryItems.example: Spectral lines are isolated by a slit + telescope.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain the dispersive power of a material and the Fraunhofer lines.
theoryItems.answer: Dispersive power ω measures how strongly a material spreads the spectrum; a material of high ω (flint glass) gives a more spread-out spectrum. Fraunhofer lines are the dark absorption lines in the solar spectrum used to label and identify colors and elements.
theoryItems.shortcut: High ω → more spread; Fraunhofer lines are the solar absorption lines.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain a spectroscope's components and use.
theoryItems.answer: A spectroscope has a collimating slit, a prism (dispersion), a telescope/eyepiece with a scale, and sometimes a compensator; it turns a prism's dispersion into a readable spectrum so one can measure a line's deviation and hence its wavelength, or compare colors.
theoryItems.shortcut: Slit + prism + telescope + scale; measure deviation.
theoryItems.example: Used to read spectra and to check lamp wavelengths.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain how a lens combination corrects chromatic aberration (achromatism).
theoryItems.answer: By joining a converging lens of one material (crown, low dispersion) to a diverging lens of another (flint, high dispersion), one can make the net power for two chosen colors equal, so their images coincide while a dispersion remains to separate colors. This is an achromatic doublet.
theoryItems.shortcut: Crown + flint cancel two-color error, keep dispersion.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T9. Why is a crown-glass lens used with a flint-glass lens in a telescope?
theoryItems.answer: Crown has a high refractive index but low dispersive power; flint has a high dispersive power. The achromatic pair makes the two colors (F and C) focus at the same point, canceling chromatic aberration while maintaining strong net magnification; this reduces colored fringes in the eyepiece.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T10. Two thin lenses: f₁ = +20 cm (crown, ω₁=0.5), f₂ = −40 cm (flint, ω₂=1.0). Find the combined focal length and check achromatic.
theoryItems.answer: 1/f = 1/20 − 1/40 = 1/40 → f = 40 cm. Achromatic: (ω₁/f₁+ω₂/f₂) = (0.5/20) + (1.0/−40) = 0.025 − 0.025 = 0 → condition satisfied; the pair is achromatic.
theoryItems.example: f = 40 cm, and the pair is achromatic.

⚡ Short / exam line:  (ω/f₁+ω′/f₂) = 0 ; net power ≠ 0.

Answer:  Marginal rays (far from the axis) of a spherical surface focus at a different point than paraxial rays, blurring the image. It is reduced by using aspherical (parabolic) surfaces, by a smaller aperture (stop) using only paraxial rays, or by combining surfaces of different shapes.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Marginal vs paraxial foci → blur.

A prism gives a 'simple' spectrum that is not pure, because different colors have different angular spreads; to obtain a pure (monochromatic) spectrum a narrow slit plus a second prism (or a lens) is used to isolate a single line.

▹ Why  (conceptual & 'why' questions)
[Why] T9. Why is a crown-glass lens used with a flint-glass lens in a telescope?

Answer:  Crown has a high refractive index but low dispersive power; flint has a high dispersive power. The achromatic pair makes the two colors (F and C) focus at the same point, canceling chromatic aberration while maintaining strong net magnification; this reduces colored fringes in the eyepiece.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Different dispersions → two-color cancellation.
Example:  Telescopes are achromatic (crown + flint) doublets.
▹ Numerical  (long numericals / problems)
